name: Range Map
why: Establish the ranges where you can score without staying available for the return.

mindset.intent: Control the space before increasing output.
mindset.focus: Notice where each fighter can land without overreaching.
mindset.reset: Return to the last range where you could see and react clearly.
mindset.anchor: Make them cross your range before they can attack.
mindset.context: Early-camp range study for a distance striker.

instructions: Mark the range where you can score while remaining difficult to reach.
Mark the range where the opponent becomes most dangerous.
Choose the strike that best controls the space between you.
Write one distance rule to test in your next technical session.
progress: Test the distance rule in technical work and keep it only if it holds up.

name: Lead-Hand Battle
why: Learn how the lead hand controls entry, rhythm and distance before exchanges develop.

mindset.intent: Own the first touch of the exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch what happens immediately after the jab or lead-hand feint.
mindset.reset: Rebuild the lead-hand position before throwing again.
mindset.anchor: Win the lead hand before chasing the rear hand.
mindset.context: Early-camp lead-hand control for a distance striker.

instructions: Identify the most common reaction to a jab or lead-hand feint.
Choose your lead-hand answer to that reaction.
Choose the follow-up that keeps you at your preferred range.
Write one lead-hand action you should avoid because it gives away distance.
progress: Use the chosen lead-hand answer during the next technical round.

name: Exit Discipline
why: Stop clean scoring from turning into avoidable return-fire by leaving on time.

mindset.intent: Finish the exchange with position, not admiration.
mindset.focus: Watch the half-second after your scoring action.
mindset.reset: If you stay too long, leave first and rebuild range.
mindset.anchor: Score, move, see again.
mindset.context: Early-camp exit habit review for a distance striker.

instructions: Find your most common exit after landing cleanly.
Spot one moment where you remain in range too long.
Choose the safer exit side for that moment.
Write one exit rule you can apply without thinking.
progress: Rehearse the exit rule after every clean score in shadow or technical work.

name: Intercept the Entry
why: Stop pressure before it reaches the pocket and takes away your preferred range.

mindset.intent: Meet the entry before it becomes an exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch the first committed step, dip, load or feint before pressure arrives.
mindset.reset: After the intercept, leave and rebuild the range immediately.
mindset.anchor: Make the entry pay before it gets close.
mindset.context: Opponent-specific entry control for a distance striker.

instructions: Identify the movement that most reliably starts the opponent's entry.
Choose one intercepting action for that trigger.
Choose the exit direction immediately after the intercept.
Define the position or distance you want to reset to.
progress: Rehearse trigger, intercept, exit and reset as one sequence.

name: Exit Lane Audit
why: Choose exits that move away from the opponent's strongest pursuit and return fire.

mindset.intent: Leave through the lane that keeps the next exchange yours.
mindset.focus: Track which direction the opponent follows fastest after you score.
mindset.reset: If the lane closes, protect first and take the next clear exit.
mindset.anchor: Do not exit into their best side.
mindset.context: SPP exit planning against the expected opponent pattern.

instructions: Choose the best exit after your jab.
Choose the best exit after your rear-hand score.
Choose the safest escape when the opponent is already pressuring.
Name the direction you should avoid because it feeds their strongest attack.
progress: Use the exit choices in technical rounds and note which lane stays open most often.

name: Rope and Corner Escape
why: Prepare a calm escape when pressure removes the open space you normally rely on.

mindset.intent: Escape before the position becomes a prolonged pocket exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch which side gets blocked first when the opponent closes the ring.
mindset.reset: Protect, create one lane, then restore long range.
mindset.anchor: One clean exit is enough.
mindset.context: SPP trapped-position planning for a distance striker.

instructions: Identify the moment the ropes or corner begin limiting your movement.
Choose the first defensive action that buys the escape.
Choose the route you will take out of the trapped position.
Define the range you want once you are clear.
progress: Start one technical round near the ropes and rehearse the same escape route.

name: First-Round Range Script
why: Confirm the opening range plan without adding new tactical information late in camp.

mindset.intent: Start simple and establish your distance early.
mindset.focus: Keep only cues you have already trained.
mindset.reset: If the opening gets messy, return to the jab and your preferred range.
mindset.anchor: Simple first, sharp second.
mindset.context: Fight-week confirmation for a distance striker.

instructions: Choose the familiar weapon you will show first.
Choose the first range test you will use to read the opponent.
Confirm your trained response if they rush the space.
Write one short first-round range cue.
progress: Rehearse the cue once in shadow work, then leave it alone.

name: Final Range Cue
why: Reduce your trained range plan to one cue you can recall under pressure.

mindset.intent: Carry one trusted range behaviour into fight day.
mindset.focus: Use only what already worked in camp.
mindset.reset: Return to the same cue after any messy exchange.
mindset.anchor: Range first.
mindset.context: Final taper compression for a distance striker.

instructions: Review one familiar clip or one successful technical round.
Choose the single range behaviour that mattered most.
Turn it into a cue of no more than six words.
progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal; do not add another.

name: Pressure Route Scan
why: Learn where opponents naturally retreat so pressure can steer instead of chase.

mindset.intent: Guide the opponent toward the space you want.
mindset.focus: Watch the first direction they choose when space disappears.
mindset.reset: If you start following, pause and rebuild the angle.
mindset.anchor: Cut the ring, do not chase it.
mindset.context: Early-camp pressure route study for a brawler.

instructions: Identify the opponent's preferred retreat direction.
Choose the direction you should step to cut that route.
Identify the cue that tells you pressure should start.
Choose the area of the ring you want to trap them in.
progress: Use one technical round to steer toward the chosen trap instead of following.

name: Safe Entry Builder
why: Build a repeatable way into the pocket without walking onto clean shots.

mindset.intent: Arrive protected before trying to win the exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch what the opponent throws as someone closes distance.
mindset.reset: If the entry is naked, leave and rebuild the setup.
mindset.anchor: Earn the pocket.
mindset.context: Early-camp entry quality for a brawler.

instructions: Choose the setup that hides your forward step.
Choose the guard position you need while crossing range.
Choose the first punch that establishes the pocket.
Define where your head should finish after the entry.
progress: Rehearse the same setup and head position before adding longer combinations.

name: Pressure Reset
why: Keep pressure controlled so forward intent does not turn into reckless chasing.

mindset.intent: Stay dangerous without becoming hurried.
mindset.focus: Spot the moment your feet begin following instead of cutting.
mindset.reset: Pause the chase, square the stance and rebuild the entry.
mindset.anchor: Pressure is position, not speed.
mindset.context: Early-camp pressure discipline for a brawler.

instructions: Find one sign that your pressure has become rushed.
Choose the safe action that pauses the chase without giving up position.
Choose the setup that starts your next entry.
Write one pressure rule that keeps your feet organised.
progress: Use the reset whenever you notice yourself following during technical work.

name: Pocket Exchange Map
why: Know what happens after the first punches so pocket exchanges stay planned rather than chaotic.

mindset.intent: Win the second decision inside the pocket.
mindset.focus: Watch the opponent's response after the first two punches.
mindset.reset: If the exchange loses shape, smother or leave instead of trading blindly.
mindset.anchor: Know the next beat.
mindset.context: SPP pocket planning for a brawler.

instructions: Identify the opponent's most common pocket sequence.
Choose your answer to that sequence.
Choose the finishing shot that best fits the opening.
Decide whether that exchange should end with an exit or a smother.
progress: Rehearse the chosen exchange ending, not just the opening combination.

name: Body Attack Opportunity
why: Find safe body attacks that reward pressure without making the entry predictable.

mindset.intent: Attack the body when the position earns it.
mindset.focus: Watch for high guards, separated elbows and upright posture.
mindset.reset: If the body line closes, go back upstairs rather than forcing it.
mindset.anchor: Open it before you take it.
mindset.context: SPP body-attack selection for a brawler.

instructions: Identify the clearest body opening the opponent gives away.
Choose the punch or feint that creates that opening.
Choose the body target you will attack.
Choose the head follow-up that punishes their reaction.
progress: Use the body attack only after the chosen setup appears in technical work.

name: Smother and Reset
why: Stop the opponent firing back immediately after your pressure combination lands.

mindset.intent: Own the space after your combination as well as during it.
mindset.focus: Watch when the opponent begins their return fire.
mindset.reset: Close the return, then rebuild before attacking again.
mindset.anchor: Finish safe before restarting.
mindset.context: SPP post-combination control for a brawler.

instructions: Choose where your body should finish after the combination.
Choose your response if the opponent fires back immediately.
Define the smother or control position you can reach safely.
Choose the action that resets you for the next pressure sequence.
progress: Finish every rehearsed combination with the same smother-or-reset decision.

name: First-Round Pressure Script
why: Confirm controlled opening pressure without turning fight-night energy into a reckless start.

mindset.intent: Take space calmly before increasing the exchange rate.
mindset.focus: Use only the pressure actions already rehearsed in camp.
mindset.reset: If you rush, rebuild the ring cut before throwing again.
mindset.anchor: Close calmly.
mindset.context: Fight-week opening script for a brawler.

instructions: Choose the opening pressure action you already trust.
Choose the first ring cut you want to establish.
Choose the first familiar combination you will show.
Write one reset cue that prevents chasing.
progress: Rehearse the script once at low intensity and keep it unchanged.

name: Final Pressure Cue
why: Reduce your pressure plan to one familiar instruction that keeps aggression organised.

mindset.intent: Carry controlled forward pressure into the fight.
mindset.focus: Keep the cue tied to positioning, not emotion.
mindset.reset: Return to the same cue whenever the pace becomes messy.
mindset.anchor: Position before volume.
mindset.context: Final taper compression for a brawler.

instructions: Review one successful pressure sequence from camp.
Choose the behaviour that made the pressure work.
Turn it into one cue of no more than six words.
progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal and do not add another.

name: Trigger Library
why: Build a clear library of movements that reliably predict an opponent's attack.

mindset.intent: Read what happens before the punch, not after it lands.
mindset.focus: Watch shoulders, weight shifts, feet and repeated rhythm changes.
mindset.reset: If the signal is unclear, observe again instead of guessing.
mindset.anchor: Read the trigger first.
mindset.context: Early-camp pattern recognition for a counter striker.

instructions: Identify the clearest signal before a jab.
Identify the clearest signal before a rear-hand attack.
Identify the clearest signal before a committed entry.
Choose the one trigger you trust most.
progress: Look only for the most reliable trigger during the next technical round.

name: Draw the Lead
why: Create predictable attacks instead of waiting passively for a counter opportunity.

mindset.intent: Make the opponent give you the attack you want.
mindset.focus: Watch what reliably makes them throw first.
mindset.reset: If the bait gets no reaction, return to neutral and show something else.
mindset.anchor: Invite, read, answer.
mindset.context: Early-camp counter creation for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose one bait or feint that invites a clear attack.
Name the attack you expect that bait to draw.
Choose the counter you will use against it.
Choose the exit that ends the exchange safely.
progress: Rehearse the bait and expected response before increasing speed.

name: Counter Activity Check
why: Keep counter striking active so patience does not become long periods of inactivity.

mindset.intent: Stay responsible for creating information.
mindset.focus: Notice when waiting stops producing useful reads.
mindset.reset: Use a safe probe when the exchange goes quiet.
mindset.anchor: Patient does not mean passive.
mindset.context: Early-camp activity control for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose one safe action that gathers information without overcommitting.
Find one moment where you waited too long to create a reaction.
Choose the action you can use to provoke a response.
Write one activity rule that keeps you engaged without forcing exchanges.
progress: Use the activity rule during quiet moments in the next technical session.

name: First Beat or Second Beat
why: Decide whether the opponent is safest to counter immediately or after they continue attacking.

mindset.intent: Counter at the beat that leaves the clearest opening.
mindset.focus: Watch whether balance and guard worsen after the first attack.
mindset.reset: If the timing is unclear, defend first and wait for the next clean read.
mindset.anchor: Choose the beat, do not rush it.
mindset.context: SPP timing selection for a counter striker.

instructions: Define when you should counter on the opponent's first attack.
Define when you should wait for their second action instead.
Choose the counter that best fits the clearer beat.
Write the safety rule that tells you when not to fire.
progress: Rehearse both beats, then keep the one that gives the cleaner exit.

name: Counter and Exit
why: Stop a successful counter from becoming a second exchange you did not choose.

mindset.intent: Treat the exit as part of the counter.
mindset.focus: Watch the opponent's first reaction after they are countered.
mindset.reset: Leave before judging how clean the counter landed.
mindset.anchor: Counter, leave, see again.
mindset.context: SPP post-counter positioning for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose the counter you expect to use most often.
Choose the exit direction that avoids the likely return.
Choose the guard position you need while leaving.
Define the distance you want before looking to counter again.
progress: Attach the same exit to the counter every time you rehearse it.

name: Counter the Counter
why: Prepare for the opponent changing their attack after your first counter starts working.

mindset.intent: Expect adaptation instead of assuming the first answer stays open.
mindset.focus: Watch what changes after the opponent has been countered once or twice.
mindset.reset: Abort if the expected adjustment does not appear.
mindset.anchor: Have an answer to their answer.
mindset.context: SPP second-order adjustment for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose the first counter you expect to establish.
Predict the most likely adjustment the opponent makes to avoid it.
Choose your second answer to that adjustment.
Define the cue that tells you to abort rather than force the sequence.
progress: Rehearse the first counter, the likely adjustment and the second answer as one decision chain.

name: First-Round Patience Script
why: Confirm active patience so the opening round gathers information without becoming passive.

mindset.intent: Create reads early without forcing the counter.
mindset.focus: Use only the baits and counters already proven in camp.
mindset.reset: If nothing appears, probe again instead of waiting empty-handed.
mindset.anchor: Active patience.
mindset.context: Fight-week opening script for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose the first safe action you will use to gather information.
Choose one familiar bait that can draw a reaction.
Confirm the counter you already trust most.
Write one activity cue that prevents passive waiting.
progress: Run the opening script once in light rehearsal and keep it unchanged.

name: Final Counter Cue
why: Reduce your counter plan to one familiar read-and-response cue for fight day.

mindset.intent: Trust the read you have already trained.
mindset.focus: Keep one trigger and one response in mind.
mindset.reset: Return to observation if the trigger is not there.
mindset.anchor: See it, answer it.
mindset.context: Final taper compression for a counter striker.

instructions: Review one successful counter sequence from camp.
Choose the trigger you recognised most reliably.
Turn the trigger and response into one cue of no more than six words.
progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal; do not add another counter idea.

name: Opponent Pattern Scan
why: Build basic tactical awareness by separating repeated patterns from one-off moments.

mindset.intent: Look for repetition before making a conclusion.
mindset.focus: Track the same behaviour across several exchanges.
mindset.reset: If the pattern appears once, keep watching before acting on it.
mindset.anchor: Repeated beats random.
mindset.context: General early-camp pattern study.

instructions: Identify the most repeated movement or exchange pattern.
Choose the clearest opportunity that pattern creates.
Choose the main danger linked to that pattern.
Write one observation to test in training rather than treating it as fact.
progress: Test the observation in technical work and keep it only if it repeats.

name: Threat Priority
why: Separate the biggest tactical problem from smaller threats so training attention stays clear.

mindset.intent: Solve the highest-value problem first.
mindset.focus: Rank threats by how often and how badly they change exchanges.
mindset.reset: If everything looks dangerous, return to frequency and consequence.
mindset.anchor: One priority first.
mindset.context: General early-camp threat ranking.

instructions: List the three threats that affect exchanges most often.
Rank them from highest to lowest priority.
Choose the first answer you will train for the top threat.
progress: Build the next tactical rehearsal around the top-ranked threat only.

name: Defensive Habit Review
why: Identify the defensive habit that restores control and the one that keeps you under pressure.

mindset.intent: See what your defence leads to, not just whether it avoids one shot.
mindset.focus: Watch the position immediately after each defensive action.
mindset.reset: Return to the defensive action that gives you sight and balance.
mindset.anchor: Defend into control.
mindset.context: General early-camp defensive habit study.

instructions: Identify your first defensive reaction under pressure.
Find the defensive habit that repeatedly leaves you in a worse position.
Choose the defensive position that restores control best.
Write one defensive rule to carry into technical work.
progress: Use the defensive rule during the next controlled pressure round.

name: Rhythm Map
why: Recognise when exchanges speed up, slow down or become predictable before adding tactics.

mindset.intent: See the tempo changes that organise the fight.
mindset.focus: Notice what happens just before the pace changes.
mindset.reset: If the rhythm becomes unclear, watch one full minute without making notes.
mindset.anchor: Tempo tells you what is next.
mindset.context: General early-camp rhythm study.

instructions: Mark one period where the pace is slow and controlled.
Mark one period where the pace suddenly rises.
Identify what usually causes the change in tempo.
Choose one rhythm you want to impose in training.
progress: Use one technical round to deliberately create the chosen rhythm.

name: First-Exchange Audit
why: Understand what repeatedly decides the first meaningful exchange before longer sequences develop.

mindset.intent: Learn what gives one fighter early control.
mindset.focus: Watch the first committed exchange after each reset.
mindset.reset: Ignore the result and look again at how the exchange started.
mindset.anchor: The start shapes the rest.
mindset.context: General early-camp opening-exchange study.

instructions: Find three first exchanges after clean resets.
Identify what action gave one fighter the advantage most often.
Identify the position that usually followed that advantage.
Choose one opening behaviour to test in training.
progress: Start three technical rounds by testing the chosen opening behaviour.

name: Position Map
why: Identify the positions where you make good decisions and the positions that create rushed choices.

mindset.intent: Know where the fight becomes easiest to read.
mindset.focus: Compare decision quality across different ring or cage positions.
mindset.reset: If a position is unclear, track what happens for the next two exchanges.
mindset.anchor: Good position buys good decisions.
mindset.context: General early-camp position study.

instructions: Choose one position where you consistently make clear decisions.
Choose one position where decisions become rushed or limited.
Identify what movement usually takes you from the bad position to the good one.
Write one positional rule to test.
progress: Use the positional rule in one controlled round and review whether it improves decision quality.

name: Reset Habit Review
why: Make the reset between exchanges deliberate instead of letting the next exchange start from disorder.

mindset.intent: Finish each exchange ready for the next one.
mindset.focus: Watch feet, guard and eyes during the reset.
mindset.reset: If one piece is missing, rebuild it before re-engaging.
mindset.anchor: Reset before restart.
mindset.context: General early-camp reset quality.

instructions: Identify the first thing you normally do after an exchange ends.
Find the part of your stance, guard or vision that is slowest to recover.
Choose the order you want your reset to happen in.
Write one short reset routine.
progress: Use the reset routine after every exchange in the next technical session.

name: Output Window Review
why: Find out when you actually work in a round instead of assuming your output is evenly spread.

mindset.intent: Know when you are working and when you are only watching.
mindset.focus: Track the moments output starts, stops and never restarts.
mindset.reset: When a quiet stretch runs long, restart with the simplest thing you own.
mindset.anchor: Silence is a decision too.
mindset.context: Early-camp work-rate study from your own footage.

instructions: Mark the point in a round where your output is highest.
Mark the longest stretch where you throw nothing at all.
Name what usually ends that quiet stretch.
Write one restart action you can use before the quiet stretch gets long.
progress: Use the restart action in the next rounds you do and note whether the quiet stretches shorten.

name: Stance and Angle Audit
why: Expose the movement direction you default to and the side of the ring or cage you keep giving away.

mindset.intent: Move on purpose rather than out of habit.
mindset.focus: Track which way your feet take you after every exchange.
mindset.reset: If you drift, square up and re-choose the direction before moving again.
mindset.anchor: Pick the angle before it picks you.
mindset.context: Early-camp movement-habit study from your own footage.

instructions: Identify the direction you circle in most often.
Identify the direction you almost never use.
Find the moment your stance stops being usable while you move.
Write one movement rule that forces you to use the neglected direction.
progress: Apply the movement rule in shadow and footwork work; keep it only if your stance stays usable.

name: Fatigue Signature Review
why: Know exactly which part of your technique fails first when you tire, so you can defend it under pressure.

mindset.intent: Protect the thing that breaks first.
mindset.focus: Compare the same action early in a round and late in a round.
mindset.reset: When the flagged fault appears, fix that one thing before anything else.
mindset.anchor: Tired is a technique problem before it is a fitness problem.
mindset.context: Early-camp fatigue study from your own late-round footage.

instructions: Pick one action you use constantly and compare it early and late in a round.
Name the first part of it that degrades when you tire.
Name what that degradation costs you defensively.
Write one cue that holds that part together late in a round.
progress: Use the cue in the last round of your next hard session and note whether the fault still appears.

name: Trigger-Response Builder
why: Turn one reliable opponent signal into a trained action instead of a vague tactical idea.

mindset.intent: Make one read immediately actionable.
mindset.focus: Choose a trigger you can genuinely see in real time.
mindset.reset: If the trigger is absent, stay neutral rather than forcing the response.
mindset.anchor: See it, do it.
mindset.context: General SPP trigger-response work.

instructions: Choose one reliable visual or positional trigger.
Choose the action you will take when it appears.
Choose how you leave after the action.
Choose what you use to reset before the next exchange.
progress: Rehearse the full trigger-response-exit-reset chain in technical work.

name: Round Flow Map
why: Understand how the opponent's behaviour changes through the round instead of treating every minute the same.

mindset.intent: Match your tactical decisions to the part of the round you are in.
mindset.focus: Compare the first, middle and final minute.
mindset.reset: If the pattern changes, update the map rather than forcing the first read.
mindset.anchor: The round has phases too.
mindset.context: General SPP round-management study.

instructions: Describe the opponent's behaviour in the first minute.
Describe what changes in the middle of the round.
Describe what changes in the final minute.
Choose the part of the round where you should take the most control.
progress: Plan one technical round around the chosen control window.

name: Scoring Map
why: Separate clean, repeatable scoring actions from busy work that looks active but gives little return.

mindset.intent: Build around actions that score clearly and leave you organised.
mindset.focus: Watch which actions land cleanly without costing position.
mindset.reset: If an action creates noise but no clean score, move on from it.
mindset.anchor: Repeat what scores cleanly.
mindset.context: General SPP scoring efficiency.

instructions: Choose the cleanest scoring action you can repeat.
Choose the position you want to control while scoring.
Choose one combination worth repeating.
Identify one busy but low-value action to reduce.
progress: Track how often the selected scoring action lands cleanly in technical work.

name: Momentum Shift Review
why: Recognise the moment control changes so you can respond before a bad spell becomes a lost round.

mindset.intent: Notice momentum early enough to act on it.
mindset.focus: Find the exchange or positional change that altered the round.
mindset.reset: Return to the last action that gave you control.
mindset.anchor: Catch the shift early.
mindset.context: General SPP momentum management.

instructions: Find the moment the round clearly changed direction.
Identify what caused the change.
Identify what the fighter gaining control noticed or exploited.
Choose the response you would use to stop the same shift.
progress: Rehearse the chosen response immediately after a deliberately difficult exchange.

name: Adversity Reset
why: Prepare a simple route back to control after being hit, trapped, tired or frustrated.

mindset.intent: Make the first action after adversity predictable and safe.
mindset.focus: Watch what successful fighters do in the first few seconds after trouble.
mindset.reset: Use the same short reset instead of solving everything at once.
mindset.anchor: First get safe, then regain control.
mindset.context: General SPP adversity planning.

instructions: Choose the immediate defensive action you use first after trouble.
Choose one short reset phrase.
Choose the next safe action that restarts your offence or position.
Choose the route that brings you back to control.
progress: Start one technical drill from a disadvantaged position and use the same reset sequence.

name: Adjustment Tree
why: Prepare one clear adjustment when the first tactical plan stops working.

mindset.intent: Change one variable instead of abandoning the whole plan.
mindset.focus: Identify exactly what is failing before choosing the adjustment.
mindset.reset: Keep the parts of the plan that are still working.
mindset.anchor: Adjust, do not panic-rewrite.
mindset.context: General SPP plan-B preparation.

instructions: Name the part of your first plan most likely to fail.
Choose the part that should stay unchanged.
Choose one tactical change that addresses the failure.
Define the sign that tells you the adjustment is working.
progress: Run one technical round where the first option is deliberately removed and use the adjustment.

name: Opening Exchange Test
why: Use the first exchanges to gather specific information instead of trying to prove the whole game plan immediately.

mindset.intent: Make the opening exchange answer one question.
mindset.focus: Choose what you need to learn first about the opponent.
mindset.reset: After the test, return to your base position before changing anything.
mindset.anchor: Test, read, then decide.
mindset.context: General SPP opening-information plan.

instructions: Choose the first tactical question you need answered.
Choose the safe action that tests that question.
Define the response that confirms your read.
Choose what you will do next if the read is confirmed.
progress: Start a technical round with the same test and act only on the observed response.

name: Route to Control
why: Link one difficult position to the position where your decisions and scoring are strongest.

mindset.intent: Know the route back to your best fighting position.
mindset.focus: Watch the movement that changes a bad position into a useful one.
mindset.reset: If the first route is blocked, protect position before trying again.
mindset.anchor: Move toward control.
mindset.context: General SPP positional transition planning.

instructions: Choose the position you most want to avoid staying in.
Choose the position where you perform best.
Identify the movement or action that links the two.
Choose one cue that starts that transition.
progress: Begin one technical drill in the difficult position and earn the route back to control.

name: Last-Minute Control
why: Plan how to close a round clearly when fatigue and urgency make decision-making noisier.

mindset.intent: Finish the round with clear control rather than random volume.
mindset.focus: Watch what changes in the final minute when both fighters know time is short.
mindset.reset: If the finish becomes reckless, return to the safest scoring action.
mindset.anchor: Close clearly.
mindset.context: General SPP final-minute management.

instructions: Identify the safest scoring action late in the round.
Choose the position you want before the final exchange.
Choose the mistake you must avoid when urgency rises.
Write one final-minute instruction.
progress: Finish one technical round using the same final-minute instruction.

name: Corner Instruction Translation
why: Turn a complicated tactical instruction into one action you can execute under fatigue.

mindset.intent: Make the instruction observable and executable.
mindset.focus: Separate what you need to notice from what you need to do.
mindset.reset: If the instruction feels crowded, reduce it to the first action only.
mindset.anchor: One instruction, one action.
mindset.context: General SPP corner-message rehearsal.

instructions: Write the full tactical instruction you want to remember.
Identify the thing you must notice before acting.
Choose the single action that follows that read.
Compress the instruction to three words.
progress: Use only the three-word version during the next hard technical round.

name: Familiar Round-One Rehearsal
why: Confirm a familiar opening sequence without adding new decisions during taper.

mindset.intent: Start with what has already worked in camp.
mindset.focus: Use only confirmed actions and responses.
mindset.reset: If the opening changes, return to the safest familiar action.
mindset.anchor: Familiar first.
mindset.context: General fight-week opening rehearsal.

instructions: Choose the first familiar action you will show.
Choose the response you already trust if the opponent disrupts it.
